title: India’s Growth Story Remains Strong, Resilient and Trustworthy Amid Global Uncertainties: Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal
subtitle:
Shri Goyal Calls for Greater Long-Term Investments and a Broader Credit Ecosystem
Shri Goyal Stresses Need for Innovative Financing Instruments to Support India’s Growth Ambitions
Shri Goyal Highlights 12 Years of Economic Reforms, Resilience and Expanding Market Opportunities
Shri Goyal Emphasises Export Growth, Manufacturing Investments and Value Addition to Make India a Global Manufacturing Hub
body_text: Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal today said that India’s growth story remained strong, resilient and trustworthy despite global uncertainties, with the country delivering on the trust placed in it by the world. Addressing the India Debt Capital Market Summit 2026, he highlighted India’s economic performance, sustained reforms, expanding trade opportunities and the growing importance of debt markets in supporting the country’s development ambitions. The Minister said India had delivered 7.8 per cent growth in the first quarter of the current financial year and expressed confidence that the country was on track to maintain its growth momentum in the second quarter as well. Gross fixed capital formation had increased by about 12 per cent, while exports had already reached USD 570 billion in the first seven months of the year. He said India was well on track to achieve its USD 1 trillion export target, which had appeared unimaginable and aspirational when it was set in May this year. Credit growth of about 19 per cent was another positive indicator, particularly for credit markets. Shri Goyal said India had demonstrated resilience amid two ongoing wars, an oil price shock, uncertainties surrounding tariffs and global trading opportunities, disruptions to sea routes and sporadic attacks affecting air travel. Despite these challenges, the world's trust in India's growth story had remained constant, and the country had delivered on that trust. He said India had continued to reform processes, introduce policies, improve ease of doing business and maintain an open-door policy to engage with businesses and stakeholders. The Government was planning for the next 20 to 25 years, with the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 firmly embedded in the system and the ambition of becoming a USD 30 trillion economy. The objective was to ensure that every child born in the country had access to a better quality of life, good education, healthcare and greater opportunities. The Minister said India had continued to finalise free trade agreements (FTAs) and reform the GST system to make it simpler and reduce tax rates, thereby boosting consumption. He noted that GST collections continued to rise, with October recording an all-time high. Exports also registered a record performance in October, reaching USD 90 billion in a single month. He said several substantive FTAs had not yet come into effect. The India-EU FTA was expected to be signed later this year and come into effect by March or April next year. The India-US trade deal was also close to culmination, with the process and pathway for finalising the agreement beginning to take shape, he added. Congratulating the organisers for bringing together the entire debt capital market ecosystem on a common platform, the Minister said the summit's theme, ‘Catalysts, Apex and Credit’, was contemporary and critical to India's growth story. He said the bond and credit markets embodied the importance of trust, as they depended on the trustworthiness of borrowers. Shri Goyal said India's trusted partnership with countries around the world was central to its engagement in preferential, bilateral and free trade agreements. The country's growth story was anchored in the vision of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the opportunities offered by a USD 4 trillion economy progressing towards USD 30 trillion, and the trusted partnerships India offered to its global partners. The Minister said India had now emerged as a preferred partner, an attractive investment destination and a trusted companion for the next two to three decades. He highlighted the country's expanding manufacturing and export capabilities, its integration with the global economy through FTAs, and the rapid development of infrastructure. He said India was expected to construct more buildings in the next 30 years than the entire existing stock of residential and commercial buildings in the country. This reflected the scale of infrastructure development and the opportunities emerging across sectors. Shri Goyal said that while rising oil prices had a significant impact on an economy, their implications for India's long-term growth needed to be assessed in the context of the country's changing economic fundamentals. He noted that India had significantly higher foreign exchange reserves, remittances and foreign direct investment inflows than it had 20 years ago. He said India was exporting over USD 700 billion, while its overall export basket was expected to reach USD 1 trillion this year. The country had a GDP of USD 4 trillion, placing it among the world's top five or six economies. On a purchasing power parity basis, India's GDP was approximately USD 18 to 19 trillion, demonstrating its capacity to absorb goods and services and produce at competitive prices. The Minister said that at India's current economic scale, fluctuations of a few dollars in oil prices could not determine the country's long-term future. He noted that India continued to have among the lowest levels of national debt in the world, with its external debt being significantly lower within its overall debt. These factors demonstrated the sustainability of India's growth story. He emphasised that India had never defaulted on its obligations to the world, including during the COVID-19 pandemic. Shri Goyal said India continued to have moderate interest rates and expressed confidence in the country's economic prospects. He noted that domestic institutional investors and retail investors had supported the markets through periods of volatility, including when foreign investors were withdrawing funds. He said India's growth story remained safe, strong, resilient and trustworthy. The Minister emphasised that India's economic transformation was the result of 12 years of sustained reforms and transformational initiatives across sectors, rather than coincidence or luck. He highlighted the Government's focus on meeting the daily needs of citizens, including food, clothing, shelter, healthcare, education, good roads, quality electricity and digital connectivity. He also highlighted the Jal Jeevan Mission's efforts to provide water to every household in every village and said that bringing 50 crore people out of poverty in 12 years was a significant achievement. As incomes rise and people move into the new middle class, middle class and upper middle class, they would create substantial market opportunities. Shri Goyal said infrastructure development, rising consumption and economic growth, together with FTAs opening up new markets, would create opportunities for India's manufacturers, agricultural exporters, seafood exporters and service providers. He expressed confidence that India would continue to grow while undertaking steady reforms and making sustained efforts to improve the lives of its people. The Minister called for taking India's exports to the next level and increasing investments in manufacturing to make the Make in India initiative a globally competitive manufacturing base. He emphasised the need for greater value addition and quality in India, along with building a larger pool of talent to enable the country to participate at the forefront of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning and quantum computing. He said India was a global partner and highlighted the expansion of its preferential market access through FTAs. Until 2014, India's FTAs covered countries with a combined GDP of approximately USD 10 trillion, against a global GDP of about USD 115 trillion. He said the nine FTAs covering 38 developed countries finalised in the last four and a half to five years covered a GDP of USD 60 trillion. Together with the earlier agreements, India now had preferential market access to economies accounting for USD 70 trillion of global GDP. The Minister said India was negotiating eight or nine additional agreements and expected to add another USD 15 trillion in market access, taking the total to USD 85 trillion out of a global GDP of USD 115 to 120 trillion. He said almost every country in the world wanted to enter into an FTA with India, reflecting the country's growing position as a trusted partner and the opportunities available for Indian businesses. Referring to the summit's theme, Shri Goyal said the Government and the private sector were collectively catalysing new growth opportunities, while opening doors for higher capital expenditure by both. The upward trend in credit growth reflected the attractiveness of India's growth story and the renewed opportunities for investment. He said the expansion of semiconductor fabrication facilities, electricity grids, data centres and the next port coming up in Vadhavan outside Mumbai would collectively generate substantial debt requirements in the economy. The Minister said debt markets would play an important role in financing India's growth and called for the country's financing system to match the scale, diversity and duration of the opportunities emerging over the next two to three decades. He emphasised the need for faster and more efficient financing, along with attractive and innovative instruments to meet the economy's debt requirements. He said private capital would become an increasingly meaningful source of capital in the coming years. India's inclusion in global bond indices would also play an important role in the growth of debt markets. The Minister outlined five key priorities for the debt capital market ecosystem: First, he called upon bond issuers, including large corporates, public sector undertakings and infrastructure developers, to make the bond market their first port of call for capital expenditure, including for longer-gestation projects. He emphasised the need to develop innovative solutions to meet their financing requirements. Second, he urged investors to support long-term debt and the broader credit ecosystem. He said insurance companies, pension companies, pension funds, provident funds and mutual funds were increasingly holding patient capital and encouraged them to look beyond AAA-rated instruments. Third, he called upon the market to make bonds easier to trade and enable transactions to take place instantaneously, on the lines of the share market. Fourth, he urged exporters and their financiers to translate the opportunities created by FTAs into investment decisions and build capacity to serve the markets that had opened up. Fifth, he reiterated that the Government was open to working with all stakeholders and invited suggestions and ideas from the sector on further reforms and improvements. The Minister concluded by expressing confidence in India's continued growth and resilience, and emphasised the importance of collaboration between the Government and the private sector in realising the country's economic ambitions. *** Abhishek Dayal/ Shabbir Azad/ Ishita Biswas
